'''Ian Barnes''' (born in [[Chadwell Heath]] in 1972) is an [[Evolutionary genetics|evolutionary geneticist]] notable for his work on [[ancient DNA]], human and animal migration, and [[phylogenetics]]. Barnes is a Research Leader in the Department of Earth Sciences at the [[Natural History Museum, London|Natural History Museum]] in London.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Prof Ian Barnes {{!}} Natural History Museum|url=https://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/departments-and-staff/staff-directory/ian-barnes.html|access-date=2022-01-04|website=www.nhm.ac.uk|language=en}}</ref>

His work on phylogenetics includes a study of South American mammal species first identified by [[Charles Darwin|Darwin]], led in collaboration with the [[University of York]], and the [[American Museum of Natural History]], which “resolved one of the last unresolved major problems in mammalian evolution: the origins of the South American native ungulates".<ref>{{Cite web|last=Dunham|first=Will|date=2015-03-19|title=Mystery of Darwin's strange South American mammals solved|url=https://www.abc.net.au/science/articles/2015/03/19/4200730.htm|access-date=2022-01-04|website=www.abc.net.au|language=en-AU}}</ref> He has also studied the phylogenetic placement of the [[Nesophontidae]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brace|first1=Selina|last2=Thomas|first2=Jessica A.|last3=Dalén|first3=Love|last4=Burger|first4=Joachim|last5=MacPhee|first5=Ross D. == Education and career ==
Barnes obtained a [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] in [[Archaeological science|Archaeological Sciences]] from the [[University of Bradford]], and a [[DPhil]] in Biology from the [[University of York]] supervised by [[Keith Dobney]]. Following his doctoral research, Barnes worked with [[Mark G. Thomas|Mark Thomas]] at [[University College London|UCL]] on the recovery of DNA from medical museum specimens, and with [[Alan J. Cooper]] at the [[University of Oxford]]. He was then awarded a [[Wellcome Trust]] Bioarchaeology Fellowship and returned to UCL, and subsequently received a [[Natural Environment Research Council|NERC]] fellowship to work on the Late Pleistocene megafauna at [[Royal Holloway, University of London]]. He was made Professor of Molecular Palaeobiology there in 2013, and moved that year to the Natural History Museum.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Professor Ian Barnes, Royal Holloway|url=https://pure.royalholloway.ac.uk/portal/en/persons/ian-barnes(f4e53f17-a02b-40cb-8eb6-eb4f349f2e7d).html}}</ref> He is the recipient of numerous research awards from major funding bodies including the Wellcome Trust and UKRI.
